meta.title: 7 million tables a day: Zerodha's report cache
meta.story: Every report a Zerodha user pulls becomes its own Postgres table, about 7 million by midnight, all thrown away at 02:00. Follow tax-deadline day, compressed (≈6 min per second by day, 1 min per second in the evening rush).

background.title: The system
background.body: Zerodha's Console serves P&L, tradebooks and tax reports to millions of users, from databases holding hundreds of billions of rows. Some reports are a one-line SELECT; others are hundreds of lines of JOINs. One finishes in 10 ms, the next takes 10 s or more. Users pull millions of them a day.

background.title: How it normally works
background.body: Console never queries the big database directly. It hands each report to DungBeetle (formerly sql-jobber) as a job. A fixed pool of workers runs at most M queries at a time on the big DB, and writes each result into a brand-new table, named after the job, in a separate Postgres 'results DB'. Console polls, then reads that table.

background.title: Today
background.body: 31 July: the income-tax filing deadline in India. Millions of users want last year's tax P&L, most of them in the evening. The clock shows India time (IST).

cast.name: console
cast.role: the app users pull reports from

cast.name: results-db
cast.role: Postgres holding one table per job

learn: why a queue in front of a big database beats more read replicas
what happens to Postgres with millions of tables
why adding workers in a rush can slow everything down
how to delete 7 million tables in a minute

dashboard.title: Requests vs completions
dashboard.why: N in, M out. When requests outrun completions, the gap goes into the queue instead of onto the big DB.

dashboard.title: Jobs queued
dashboard.why: Where a rush waits. A growing queue is the system saying 'later', not failing.

dashboard.title: Report wait p95
dashboard.why: What users feel: how long 'your report is being generated' lasts.

dashboard.title: ledger-db CPU
dashboard.why: The expensive DB. If it stays flat during a rush, the queue is doing its job.

dashboard.title: ledger-db queries in flight
dashboard.why: The M in 'N requests, M queries'. It should never pass the worker cap.

dashboard.title: Tables in results-db
dashboard.why: One brand-new table per finished job. Climbs all day, never shrinks until the nightly wipe.

dashboard.title: System catalog size
dashboard.why: Postgres's own bookkeeping (pg_attribute, pg_class, pg_index) for millions of tables.

dashboard.title: Results volume used
dashboard.why: The day's results on one EBS volume. It only has to last until 02:00.

dashboard.title: Report fetch p99
dashboard.why: SELECT * from a job's own table. If millions of tables hurt Postgres, it would show here first.

dashboard.title: pg_class rows
dashboard.why: About three relations per result table: the heap, its TOAST table and the TOAST index.

dashboard.title: ledger-db query p99
dashboard.why: Per-query time on the big DB. Past the core count, more concurrency makes every query slower.

dashboard.title: ledger-db temp-file spill
dashboard.why: Sorts and hashes that no longer fit in work_mem write to disk: the sign of too many big queries at once.

dashboard.title: CREATE TABLE + COPY time
dashboard.why: The cost of writing one job's result as a new table. Stays in milliseconds even at 7 M tables.

dashboard.title: results-db CPU
dashboard.why: Rules out the results DB as the bottleneck: 64 vCPUs mostly idle even in the rush.

beat.hint: Console never queries the big ledger-db itself. It asks dungbeetle to run a named SQL report as a job. A worker runs it on ledger-db and writes the rows into a brand-new table in results-db, named after the job. Console then just reads that table. It is 08:00 on 31 July and results-db is empty.
beat.deep: Tasks are named queries in a .sql file (-- name: get_tax_pnl, -- db: ledger-db). A job is one run of a task with args: POST /tasks/get_tax_pnl/jobs.

notes.text: Requests ≈ completions: every job runs straight away
results-db starts the day empty: 0 tables

feed.text: morning. 31 July, ITR filing deadline. expect a big evening on tax P&L reports
09:48 IST GET /reports/tax-pnl?fy=2023-24 → job tax_pnl_ZX4821_fy24 queued (202 Accepted)
job tax_pnl_ZX4821_fy24 SUCCESS rows=2,184 in 412ms → CREATE TABLE "tax_pnl_ZX4821_fy24" (7 cols)
LOG: statement: SELECT * FROM "tax_pnl_ZX4821_fy24" ORDER BY trade_date  (2,184 rows, 1.8 ms)
$ psql results -c "SELECT count(*) FROM pg_class WHERE relkind='r'"  → 1,288,410

beat.hint: By 2 pm about 1.4 million reports have run, and each became its own table, sized 1,000 to 5,000 rows. Reading a report is a SELECT * from that small table: no index, no JOIN, no other user's rows in the way. Columns come straight from the query's result.
beat.deep: Column types are mapped from the result set (INT8→BIGINT, NUMERIC→DECIMAL, TIMESTAMP, DATE, BOOLEAN, everything else TEXT). TEXT columns give each table a TOAST table + index too.

notes.text: ~1.4 M tables by 2 pm, one per finished job
Fetch stays ~2 ms: each report is its own small table
Only ~35 queries in flight on the big DB
≈3 relations per table: heap + TOAST table + index

feed.text: 15:30 market closed. ~1.9M report tables so far, ledger-db at 40%. calm before the evening
18:02 IST tax-pnl requests 3× the 17:00 rate (pre-deadline filing)
heavy queue: 150/150 workers busy, light 50/50, pending=12,406
$ curl -s localhost:6060/jobs/queue/heavy | jq length  → 58,213

beat.hint: Requests hit 520 a second, but 200 workers can only finish about 400. The rest wait in the queue, and users see 'Your report is being generated'. ledger-db does not notice: it never runs more than 200 queries. This is the design working. The rush lands on a queue, not on the database.
beat.deep: Throughput ceiling ≈ workers ÷ mean job time = 200 ÷ ~0.5 s ≈ 400 jobs/s. Queue grows at (520 − 400) × 60 s ≈ 7,200 jobs per minute of story time.

notes.text: 520/s in vs ~400/s that 200 workers can finish
The excess piles up here: ~106k jobs waiting
Flat at ~72%: the big DB never sees the rush
Users wait ~4–5 min instead of timing out

feed.text: tickets coming in: 'tax P&L stuck on being generated for 10 mins'. filing deadline is tonight
queue is past 200k and it's deadline day. bumping heavy worker concurrency 30 → 90 on all 5 nodes, ledger-db has headroom
dungbeetle: --worker-concurrency 30 → 90 (heavy queue), rolling restart
LOG: temporary file: path "base/pgsql_tmp/pgsql_tmp41822.17", size 1342177280

beat.hint: Tripling the workers sent 500 heavy reports at ledger-db at once. Its 64 cores are pinned, queries trip over each other, and completions fall from 400 to about 290 a second. The queue now grows faster than before. Past the database's limit, more concurrency means less throughput.
beat.deep: ledger-db runs work_mem=600MB. At 200 queries that is fine; at 500 the sorts and hashes no longer fit in 128 GB RAM and spill to pgsql_tmp. Query p99 goes from ~1.4 s to ~9 s.

notes.text: Pinned near 100%: 500 heavy queries on 64 cores
Completions fall to ~290/s: more workers, less done
Queue grows faster: ~450k
600 MB work_mem × 500 queries: sorts spill to disk

feed.text: ledger-db at 100% and completions went *down*. reverting to 30
dungbeetle: --worker-concurrency 90 → 30 (heavy queue), rolling restart
LOG: checkpoint complete; temp files 0 B in last 60 s
20:05 IST tax-pnl request rate falling: 330/s (from 520/s peak)

timeline.title: Back to M: the queue drains

beat.hint: Back at 200 workers, ledger-db finishes ~400 reports a second again, and the rush is fading. Requests now arrive slower than they finish, so the queue shrinks by roughly 100 jobs a second. Nothing was lost: every queued job will still get its own table.
beat.deep: Queue peaked near 680k at ~19:58. With requests at ~300/s and completions at 400/s, the backlog drains in about an hour of story time.

notes.text: Past the peak (~680k) and shrinking
Completions back at ~400/s, requests now below
Back to ~72%: the cap protects the big DB again
p99 back to ~1.4 s once spills stop

feed.text: $ curl -s localhost:6060/jobs/queue/heavy | jq length  → 468,571
wait is under 15 min again. lesson learned: the cap is the feature
21:15 IST heavy queue drained (pending=0); 6.4M jobs completed today
$ psql results -c "SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(oid)) FROM pg_class WHERE relname IN ('pg_attribute','pg_class','pg_index')"  → 47 GB · 9 GB · 2.4 GB

beat.hint: Near midnight results-db holds about 7 million tables and 60 GB of catalog: Postgres's own records of every table and column. Report fetches are still about 2 ms. Postgres finds a table by name through an index on its catalog, so 7 million of them cost disk space, not speed.
beat.deep: pg_attribute ~48 GB (one row per column, system columns included), pg_class ~9 GB (~21 M relations), pg_index ~2.5 GB though DungBeetle makes no indexes: likely the TOAST indexes. Each backend caches only the relations it touches.

notes.text: ~7 M tables, each one finished report
~60 GB of catalog, mostly pg_attribute
Fetch still ~2 ms: lookups go by name, through an index
~21 M relations: 3 per table

feed.text: 23:35 IST EOD exchange import started (bulk COPY into tradebook_2024_07)
midnight. deadline passed. 7.2M report tables today, a record. wipe runs at 02:00 as usual
02:00:04 IST nightly-wipe started on results-db (vol-a → vol-b)
02:00:12 $ pg_ctl -D /data/pg stop -m fast  → server stopped
02:00:28 $ umount /data && aws ec2 detach-volume --volume-id vol-a  → detached
02:00:44 $ aws ec2 attach-volume --volume-id vol-b --device /dev/sdf && mount /data  → ok
02:01:00 $ pg_ctl -D /data/pg start  → database system is ready to accept connections

beat.hint: Deleting 7 million tables one by one would take hours and leave a bloated catalog to vacuum. Instead the cron job stops Postgres, detaches the full volume, attaches an empty one and starts again, in about a minute. The few jobs that arrived meanwhile waited in the queue.
beat.deep: DROP TABLE × 7.2 M deletes ~21 M pg_class and ~200 M pg_attribute rows, all dead tuples needing VACUUM, plus ~21 M file unlinks. A volume swap touches none of it. This only works because results are disposable: fsync=off, no replica.

notes.text: 7.2 M tables gone in one volume swap
60 GB of catalog gone, no VACUUM needed
~200 jobs waited out the 48 s restart
Fresh 2 TB volume, empty

feed.text: 02:58 IST vol-a reformatted; empty cluster restored; kept as tomorrow's spare
08:40, Aug 1. results-db at ~120k tables, vol-a on standby. market opens 09:15

report.tldr: Zerodha queues every report and lets only M queries reach the big DB, writing each result into its own throwaway Postgres table. ~7 M tables a day are cheap to read and free to delete: the whole volume is swapped out every night.

chain.text: Tax-deadline rush: 520 report requests a second at peak
DungBeetle queues the excess; only 200 queries reach ledger-db
Workers raised to 500: ledger-db saturates, throughput drops to ~290/s
Back to 200 workers: ~400/s again, the queue drains
Each finished job becomes a table: 7.2 M tables, 60 GB of catalog
02:00: stop, swap the EBS volume, start. Empty in about a minute

learnings.title: Put a queue in front of big DBs
learnings.body: Users are N and unbounded; the database is M. Accept every request, but send at most M queries and let the rest wait.

learnings.title: Past the cap, more workers is less
learnings.body: Once the DB's cores and memory are full, extra concurrency adds contention and disk spills. Throughput falls.

learnings.title: Shape the cache like the read
learnings.body: One small table per report makes reads a plain SELECT *, with sorting and filtering on a few thousand rows.

learnings.title: Delete disposable data in bulk
learnings.body: Don't drop 7 M tables; throw away the volume. Treat the results DB like a cache: fsync off, no replica, rebuilt nightly.

math.title: Back of the envelope
lines: 7.2 M jobs ÷ ~14 busy hours      ≈ 140 jobs/s average; evening peak 520/s
200 workers ÷ ~0.5 s per job       ≈ 400 jobs/s ceiling (M)
(520 − 400) jobs/s × 40 min        ≈ 290k jobs queued, not 290k extra queries
60 GB catalog ÷ 7.2 M tables       ≈ 8 KB of metadata per table
DROP TABLE × 7.2 M at ~2 ms (rough) ≈ 4 h + VACUUM; volume swap ≈ 1 min

myths.myth: Millions of tables will melt Postgres.
myths.truth: A table is found by name through an index on pg_class, and each backend caches only what it touches. The cost is disk (60 GB of catalog), not query speed.

myths.myth: Deadline day needs more workers or read replicas.
myths.truth: The big DB's capacity is the limit. More concurrency past it slows every query; the queue already absorbs the rush.

myths.myth: One big results table with a job_id column would be cleaner.
myths.truth: Every report has different columns, and deleting rows leaves bloat to vacuum. Separate tables get their schema for free and disappear with the volume.

config: -- name: get_tax_pnl  /  -- db: ledger-db  /  -- queue: heavy      # task header in reports.sql
ledger-db: work_mem = 600MB          # fine at 200 queries, spills at 500
results-db: fsync = off, synchronous_commit = off, no replication  # data is disposable
results-db: work_mem = a few MB      # no JOINs, just SELECT * on small tables
results-db: shared_buffers sized to the tables created in the peak hour
runbook: Queue growing but ledger-db flat? That is the design working; watch report wait, not the queue size.
Never raise worker concurrency without checking ledger-db CPU, temp-file spill and query p99.
Keep the volume well under 2 TB on peak days; size from the record day, not the average.
If the wipe fails, dungbeetle holds jobs in Redis: fix the mount, then start Postgres.
